chief_complaint: chronic bloating, loose stools, and extreme fatigue for 6 months
hpi_details: 6-month history of postprandial abdominal bloating, excessive flatulence, and 2-3 bulky, foul-smelling, pale stools per day. Reports profound fatigue and brain fog. Has an intensely itchy, blistering rash over both elbows for the past month. No blood in stool.
ideas: thinks she might be allergic to dairy or wheat after talking to friends
concerns: worried her constant fatigue is damaging her performance at her new job
expectations: wants blood tests for food intolerances and advice on supplements
pmh: type 1 diabetes since age 12, iron deficiency anaemia treated intermittently with oral iron
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks alcohol rarely, works as a graphic designer

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Coeliac Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Check coeliac serology while patient remains on a gluten-containing diet (critical instructions), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chronic bloating, loose stools, and extreme fatigue for 6 months

Key HPI features: 6-month history of postprandial abdominal bloating, excessive flatulence, and 2-3 bulky, foul-smelling, pale stools per day. Reports profound fatigue and brain fog. Has an intensely itchy, blistering rash over both elbows for the past month. No blood in stool.

Objective/Exam findings: Check BMI, conjunctival pallor, inspect extensor rash on elbows. Serology: total IgE/IgA, anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTg IgA), FBC, ferritin, folate, B12, bone profile.
Relevant background/PMH: type 1 diabetes since age 12, iron deficiency anaemia treated intermittently with oral iron
Current medications: insulin glargine, insulin lispro
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Coeliac Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Irritable bowel syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: bloody or nocturnal diarrhoea, signs of severe malabsorption (marked weight loss, anaemia, low bone density), or persistent symptoms despite a gluten-free diet.
management_principles: Check coeliac serology while patient remains on a gluten-containing diet (critical instructions)
Refer for duodenal biopsy via gastroscopy for confirmation
Dermatology referral for skin biopsy if needed
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 29F with T1DM presents with chronic steatorrhoea, bloating, fatigue, and an itchy extensor rash (dermatitis herpetiformis) over 6 months. History of iron deficiency anaemia.
reference_soap.objective: Check BMI, conjunctival pallor, inspect extensor rash on elbows. Serology: total IgE/IgA, anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTg IgA), FBC, ferritin, folate, B12, bone profile.
reference_soap.assessment: Coeliac disease with likely dermatitis herpetiformis and malabsorption. DDx: irritable bowel syndrome, Giardia lamblia infection, inflammatory bowel disease, lactose intolerance.
reference_soap.plan: Check coeliac serology while patient remains on a gluten-containing diet (critical instructions). Refer for duodenal biopsy via gastroscopy for confirmation. Dermatology referral for skin biopsy if needed. Dietitian referral once confirmed.

learning_objectives: Identify autoimmune comorbidities associated with coeliac disease (Type 1 Diabetes, autoimmune thyroiditis)
Recognise extraintestinal manifestations of malabsorption (anaemia, dermatitis herpetiformis, fatigue)
Explain the critical importance of continuing gluten consumption prior to serological testing and biopsy
Address patient expectations regarding dietary modification and diagnostic accuracy

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune reaction to gluten damages the small bowel lining, causing bloating, fatty pale stools, and malabsorption of nutrients like iron.
red_flags: Bloody or nocturnal diarrhoea — atypical for coeliac disease and should prompt evaluation for IBD
Signs of severe malabsorption (marked weight loss, anaemia, low bone density)
Persistent symptoms despite a gluten-free diet — raises concern for refractory coeliac disease

must_ask.say: Are your stools bulky, pale, and foul-smelling, and do they float?
Do your symptoms seem to get worse after eating bread, pasta, or other wheat foods?
Can you tell me about the rash on your elbows — is it itchy or blistering?
How would you describe the tiredness — is it affecting your concentration too?
Have you been told before that your iron levels are low?
Does anyone in your family have coeliac disease, diabetes, or thyroid problems?

history.answer: I've been feeling constantly bloated and having loose stools for the past six months, and I'm exhausted all the time.
It started gradually about six months ago and has been happening almost every single day since then.
I have loose bowel movements two to three times a day. They are bulky, pale, very foul-smelling, and often float and are hard to flush away.
No, I have never seen any blood or mucus in my stool.
No, I never wake up in the middle of the night having to go to the bathroom.
I don't have severe cramping pain or a constant urge to strain, just very uncomfortable bloating and excess gas after I eat.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting.
No, I don't feel lightheaded, my mouth isn't dry, and I've been drinking plenty of fluids and urinating normally.
No, I haven't eaten any raw seafood or buffet food, and none of my coworkers or friends have had any stomach bugs.
No, I haven't traveled anywhere recently, and I haven't gone camping or drunk any untreated water.
No, I haven't taken any antibiotics recently, and I haven't been admitted to the hospital.
I've unintentionally lost about three kilograms over the past few months even though my appetite is fine.
The bloating and gas definitely feel worse after meals, especially when I eat bread, pasta, or dairy products.
I started a new job recently so there is some stress, but the diarrhea is steady every day and never alternates with constipation.
About a month ago, I broke out in an intensely itchy, blistering rash over both of my elbows. I don't have any joint pain, mouth ulcers, or eye redness.
No, I haven't had heart palpitations, heat intolerance, shakiness, or facial flushing.
I feel completely drained of energy all day long, and I've been having trouble concentrating and thinking clearly at work.
I was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia a couple of years ago and took iron pills, but my iron levels seem to drop back down whenever I stop.
Some friends suggested I might have an allergy or intolerance to wheat or dairy, and I'm really worried my fatigue is hurting my performance at my new job.
I'd like to get tested to see if I have a food intolerance and find out which vitamin supplements I should be taking.
I have had type 1 diabetes since I was 12 years old, as well as recurring iron deficiency anemia.
I haven't had any surgeries; I was only hospitalized once when my diabetes was first diagnosed in childhood.
I take long-acting insulin glargine once daily at night, rapid-acting insulin lispro with my meals, and occasional oral iron tablets.
No, I don't have any allergies to medications.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes.
I rarely drink alcohol, maybe one glass of wine every few months on special occasions.
I work full-time as a graphic designer at an advertising firm and live alone in an apartment.
My mother has an autoimmune thyroid condition, Hashimoto's disease, but no one in my family has celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or bowel cancer.
My last period started two weeks ago and my cycles are regular. I use condoms with my partner, and there is no possibility that I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Patient appears fatigued and mildly pale with a low-normal body mass index, but is in no acute distress.
Blood pressure is 112/72 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Blood pressure and heart rate remain stable upon standing, with no significant postural drop.
Mild conjunctival pallor is present bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
Oral mucous membranes are moist with no aphthous ulcers or glossitis.
Slight generalized abdominal distension is visible; no surgical scars, caput medusae, or hernia noted.
Normal to slightly hyperactive bowel sounds present in all four quadrants without vascular bruits.
Abdomen is soft with mild diffuse fullness, but without localized tenderness, guarding, rigidity, or palpable masses.
No rebound tenderness in any abdominal quadrant.
Symmetrical clusters of excoriated, erythematous papulovesicles over the extensor surfaces of both elbows; normal skin turgor without signs of dehydration.
Normal anal sphincter tone without fissures or hemorrhoids, and digital examination reveals pale, pasty stool without visible blood.
